title: SkyLink Airlines: growing revenue, sinking profit
prompt: Our client is SkyLink, a regional airline flying short routes in the Midwest. Revenue grew last year, but the airline went from a small profit to a loss. The board wants to understand what happened and what to do about it.

clarifying_answers.geography: Midwest US, short routes under two hours.
clarifying_answers.business_model: Ticket sales plus small bag and seat fees. All planes are the same model.
clarifying_answers.timeline: Board wants a plan for next year.
clarifying_answers.changes: SkyLink expanded its route network last year.

hidden_facts.hint: revenue, sales growth, or where growth came from
hidden_facts.fact: Revenue grew from $800M to $880M. All of that growth came from 6 new routes. Revenue on existing routes was flat.

hidden_facts.hint: costs, cost breakdown, or cost growth
hidden_facts.fact: Total costs grew from $780M to $900M. Fuel costs on the existing network went up $30M, and the new routes cost $90M to operate.

hidden_facts.hint: how the new routes are performing, load factor, or how full planes are
hidden_facts.fact: The 6 new routes bring in $80M of revenue combined. Planes on new routes are 55% full on average (load factor), versus 82% on existing routes.
Jet fuel prices rose 12% last year. SkyLink does not hedge its fuel.

hidden_facts.hint: competitors or fares on the new routes
hidden_facts.fact: On 4 of the 6 new routes, a low-cost carrier already flies, with fares about 20% below SkyLink's.

math_answers.question: How big was the swing in profit from last year to this year?
What profit or loss do the new routes make?
Assuming revenue grows with how full the planes are, what load factor would the new routes need to break even?

ideal_structure: Profit swing = change in revenue - change in costs
Split the network: existing routes vs new routes
Existing routes: revenue flat, fuel cost up
New routes: revenue, cost, load factor, competition
Options: cut or fix weak routes, fuel hedging, pricing
recommendation: The $40M profit swing has two parts: $30M from unhedged fuel on existing routes, and a $10M loss on the new routes, which are only 55% full against a break-even of about 62%. Exit or reschedule the new routes where a low-cost carrier competes, keep the ones near break-even, and start a fuel hedging program.
common_mistakes: Missing that revenue growth came entirely from loss-making routes
Not computing a break-even load factor
